description: Placeholder Kanji

We start our journey of over 2000 kanji with a single stroke. The kanji for one is but a single horizontal line written from left to right. Any learner of Japanese will likely have encountered this kanji as one of, if not the first kanji they learn, and it is easy to see why.

The character for two is, unsurprisingly, made up of two lines. The top line, which is written first, is also slightly shorter than the below line. Though Japanese still use kanji to represent numbers, depending on the context, Arabic numerals are also commonly used, so don't be surprised if you see a '2' appear when perusing a Japanese text.
The character for three is made up of a three horizontal lines. Once again, pay close attention to the size of each line when writing out this kanji.

If you were expecting a kanji with four lines to continue the pattern, then you will be disappointed by this kanji. In general, a kanji won't be introduced without first introudcing the elements that comprise it, but an exception has been made for the kanji relating to numbers. The character shows two 'human legs' which have been 'pent in' by a box-shaped enclosure.

This somewhat unique collection of strokes represents the number five. If you cover up the left had side of this kanji, you can sort of make out the Arabic numeral 5. This one may be a bit of a stretch but this should help you keep this kanji apart from the other numbers.

The kanji for six is actually made up of two elements 'pot lid' and 'animal legs', both of which we will learn in the next few chapters. For now, just remember the four strokes that make up this kanji.
This character for seven has the visual appearance of a so-called 'French seven' that has been flipped upside down.
This character, representing eight, also consists of two strokes, though this time they do not intersect.
Keep the stroke order in mind when learning this kanji to help keep it distinct from the similar looking kanji 力.
Another two stroke kanji, only this time the strokes form a very simple plus shape.
A simple pictogram of an open mouth. The stroke order is exactly the same as with 四 except for the dangling 'human legs'.
To keep this kanji distinct from 口, a single line was added before the final bottom stroke.
vocabulary: 一日・いちにち・ついたち

description: The first stroke for this kanji curves to the left in much the same way as the first stroke of 九 does. This kanji is a pictogram of a moon.
The kanji for evening also represents a moon. Here the moon is somewhat distorted when compared to 月, almost as though the evening has not yet fully surrended to the night.
This kanji represents a rice field that has been split into four. Pay close attention to the stroke order whne writing this kanji.

This kanji is a pictogram of a tree. The first stroke represents the leafy boughs of the tree, with the second stroke representing its trunk. Finally the two downward sweeping strokes represent the trees roots anchoring it down.
The three vertical parts of this kanji represent three mountain peaks with the central peak being taller than the other two.
Keep this character distinct from 右, by making sure the second stroke does not cross above the first. Here the small 'mouth' is representative of a little 'stone'.
The kanji for eye looks similar to 日 but with two inner strokes instead of one. Imagine the two inner strokes representing two eyelids with an invisible pupil interposed between them.

The kanji for shellfish itself consists of the element for 'eye' and the 'animal legs' we encountered in 六. The kanji represents a pictogram of the shell of a shellfish with two small legs to help it walk on the sea floor.
Whether this kanji represents a bent arm or a plow is still debated, but this kanji is used for the idea of 'power'.

Here we see a 'mouth' with sound waves coming out as represented by the first four strokes. Note that in print, the first stroke appears as a vertical stroke, but when written by hand the stroke is written as downward 'drop'. From time to time, we will see that the print form of a kanji doesn't always match up with how it would be written by hand.
Combining the characters for the sun 日 and moon 月 creates a kanji meaning 'bright'. It's easy to relate this kanji to the two brightest things seen within the sky, those being the sun and the moon.

The kanji for 'old' is made up of the elements 'ten' and 'mouth'. Instead of using these keywords, it may be best to think of the 'ten' as a 'cross'-shaped gravestone above an opening in the ground which presumably leads to an old crypt. Here we see why sometimes having more than one name or idea associated with an element can help create a more memorable mnemonic.
This kanji depicts a 'sun' rising over a 'cross' creating the picture of church bells ringing out in the early morning.
A 'male' is depicted here as someone flexing their arm in a rice field, providing the physical strength for the harvest.
A rock is simply a stone the size of a mountain. This kanji really needs no further explanation.
This kanji represents quite an abstract concept. Imagine a forrest containing trees with eyes which watch over each other. Each tree watches another tree to ensure their mutual safety.
A tree with a line striking through its trunk came to mean 'book'. Imagine a tree being chopped down near the roots, the wood later being used to create the paper for the books.

This kanji always reminds me of one of those complicated architectural blueprints with lots of annotating 'words', 'crosses' indicating the important parts of the plan, and of course the all important measurements.

'Say five mouths' clearly refers to the five senses used to fully communicate across a language barrier. Of course we must use our mouths to say words, but we must also use our other senses to fully appreciate the language and culture.

A 'mouth' above a 'shellfish' could represent someone eating lots of seafood, but here, the mouth is in fact eating all the 'money' generated by the company they work for, presumably to the dismay of the big bosses.
Imagine an evening so 'dark' that the only way to identify your friend in a crowd is if they open their 'mouth' and say their name.
Sometimes, the simple reduplication of an element can create a new kanji. Here we have 'evening' written twice to mean 'many', demonstrating the many evenings we have to rest.
'Mouth' is reduplicated here three times to create a kanji meaning 'goods'. When buying new goods, it's important to think of how many mouths you need to feed in order to purchase the correct amount.

The kanji for 'nine' is here accompanied by a single drop that changes the meaning entirely into that of 'Round'. Though this kanji refers to the shape of something, a number can too be considered 'round'. Here we turn 'nine' into a round number by adding a small 'drop'.
The only difference between the kanji for 'sun' and 'white' is the presence of the small 'drop' on top. To protect our skin from the 'sun', we often apply a 'drop' of white sunscreen.
'One' plus 'white', makes a hundred. One can imagine that the number 'one' sunscreen blocks 100% of the sun's rays.

It might be easier to think of this as a 'drop' + 'ten', though it can be broken down further to reveal the walking stick that is being driven through the horizontal floor through the power of a thousand drops.
You can break this down into its elements if you wish, but it might be easier to see this as simply a line passing through an opening marking its middle.

A pole accompanied by two small drops. Note how the drops are written after the central vertical stroke, and also that the central stroke contains a little hook at the end. The smallness here refers to the small drops, presumably small side effects caused by the larger central stroke.
Small plus an extra drop makes 'few'. Imagine a few drops of water hitting a window. After a while, the drops will slide down the window, creating a trail represnted by the final stroke.
Once again, you can break this down into its components if you wish, but this kanji symbolically represents a small line raised 'above' a larger line.
In contrast to the previous kanji, the small line now resides 'below' the large line. These two kanji become easier to remember when learned as a pair.
Have you ever been at a gathering or party that is lasting way too long into the evening? Well this magic wand allows you to teleport outside. The catch is that it only works in the evening.
Here a walking stick with a magic wand attached that automatically 'stops' things for the user.

We combine the elements for 'stop' and 'a few' that we just encountered to create the kanji for 'walk'. The etymological form of the stop element being a 'footprint' comes in handy here. We see 'a few footprints' to indicate where someone has been walking.
This kanji represents the 'correct' way to start a race, with the footprint just before the line. After all, putting your foot over the line before the race starts would not be correct.
Oneself here is represented by a single drop over an eye. If you've ever tried to put eye drops in, you'd know it can sometimes by tricky to administer them by oneself.
The kanji for mother here is a pictogram of two breasts. Take good care with the stroke order here; this is not the simple 'mouth' shape we are used to dealing with.
Every mother deserves a lie down. Or perhaps this kanji represents the collective experience of every mother having a child lie down on top of them.

The pictogram of a father here is considerably more abstract than that for mother. It might be easier to see the father's face here though, the two eyes represented by the first two strokes and then a nose that forms the outline of a moustache with the last two strokes.

A father with a pot lid on his head represents the idea of mingling or the meeting of people. Here we see a father who has put a pot lid on his head so that he can stand out in the crowd whilst mingling with other fathers.

A school is obviously a place where lots of pupils mingle, but what does this have to do with trees? Perhaps it is a really old building made from wood, or the tree represents the growth of the pupils whilst in attendance. However you imagine it, combine these two elements to create the kanji for school.

Be careful with the stroke order with this kanji. Here we see a strange conglomeration of strokes that look like elements. Can you see 'lie down', 'walking stick', perhaps the outline of 'correct' or 'stop'. This kanji is one of those rare occasions where simply learning the kanji as a unit is probably the simplest path forward.
The kanji for person is simply a pictogram of a person with two outsrtetched legs.
Here we see a pictogram of your chosen 'person' from the previous kanji resting against a 'tree'.

The kanji for 'body' differs from 'rest' by a single stroke. We saw this combination of 'tree' and 'one' earlier in the kanji for book. In a similar way to reading a book, you can tell a lot about a person by reading their body language.
This kanji has a striking resemblance to 'small', 小, except where the central stick in 'small' only produced two small drops, here we see two large splashes of water.
The kanji for ice is simply the kanji for water but with an extra drop. Now the form almost represents a snowflake.

'Water', 'drop', 'water', almost seems to tell the story of someone swimming. Notice how the vertical stroke appears to have a small handle at the top this time. We will encounter the right-hand side as a standalone kanji later.
The ultimate destination of each and every drop of water is ultimately the sea.
We see an old, possibly ancient, ritual of admiring the moon's reflection in the waters of a lake.
The idea of this kanji is something running alongside something else, or in accordance with. The kanji represnts this as water running alongside a gully.
Here an unfortunate execusion decision is to be made, either by water or by the guillotine.
Here we see a pictogram of a fire, or perhaps a person on fire! The two drops represent the smoke rising up from the flames.
This kanji separates itself from the traditional wet rice field with the addition of the 'fire' element to indicate a dry field.
For this kanji, imagine two people discussing something with such passion that they have burst into two flames. The contribution of the 'say' element here should be obvious.

Here we see the form that the fire element takes when it appears at the bottom of the kanji. We might have to work a little harder to make some seemingly nonsensicle pnemonics to stick in our minds. Here, a wizard waves his 'magic wand', and spits 'fire' straight from his 'mouth'. The fire reduces its target to a single Spot of ash.

The stroke order for this kanji follows the typical progression from left to right. You might be able to see the main structure of a human heart with its various adjoining veins and arteries represented by the remaining three strokes.
It might be helpful to think of the 'rice field' as a sort of brain in this kanji. We then have the two ways people tend to think, either with their brain or with their heart.

The top half of this kanji contains the familiar 'tree' and 'eye' combination as seen in mutual (K-0028). We can therefore continue our story of the 'trees with eyes' to cover our new kanji. The forest of 'trees with eyes' actually has a certral hub at the 'heart' of the forest to which all the trees are connected to. This is where all the 'thoughts' from the trees are processed.

You may recall from frame 'E-031' that we could attach the meaning of 'nose' to the usual kanji meaning 'oneself'. Here, the association becomes particularly useful. To check that someone is still alive, check that their 'nose' and 'heart' are both 'breathing'. Consider that a heartbeat is, in a way, a 'breath of life'
You would think that the 'state of mind' you'd feel when faced with the 'guillotine' is far from pleasant. Perhaps this instead represents the state of mind of the macarbe on-lookers instead.
The kanji for bamboo is indeed two stalks of bamboo with attached leaves at the top. Notice the way the second stork has a slight uptick at the bottom, whilst the first does not.
Once again, the trees with eyes make an appearance. This time, the trees and bamboo are intertwining to form the shape of a box, or pehaps Pandora's box to enclose a sinister curse.

This kanji represents two strands of intertwining string that has become incredibly stylised over time. The first three strokes are quite unique, with the final three strokes appearing similar to 'small' without the hook on the central stroke.
Add a drop to the thread to get the more abstract idea of a lineage. It's easy to imagine the metaphorical thread holding the people (here rerpresented by a drop) in a family lineage together.
A new fad diet involves growing your food a rice field that is so thin that it is the width of a piece of thread.
The kanji here gets the image of a line by considering the white, thread-like line of white foam that appears on the waters of crashing ocean waves.
The person in charge here is a person who presides over an entire lineage.

Combine the kanji for 'two' with the element of 'small' to get 'show off'. Try to think of this as a pictogram of an altar or small table meant to display something. The table has small tassles falling down the sides of it to exemplify the object's special nature.

The right hand side of the kanji has an elaborate but recurring arrangement of elements. We have 'one', 'mouth' and 'rice field', a rice field so full that it can fill every one person's mouth. On the left, we have the shape-shifted 'altar' element. Combining everything together, we can imagine an offering from the bountiful rice field on the right, placed on the altar on the left in the hopes of incurring a blessing.
Originally a pictogram of a cow's face with horns, the kanji has since become heavily styalised and reduced to the strokes for 'lie down' and 'ten'.

This kanji represnt the idea of a physical and 'tangible thing'. We will see the kanji for a 'hypothetical thing' later in this section. Though it may be a bit abstract, a cow and a bloody knife form the basis of an obvious story.
Originally a pictogram of a snake, however this kanji now refers to an insect. The kanji contains 'middle', with two extra strokes at the bottom.
This is the full kanji from which the wind element gets its name. Pay close attention to the extra drop above the 'insect' element.
This kanji is a pictogram of rowboat. The first stroke represents the boat's rudder (or perhaps properller). Inside we see a person sitting with a oar sticking out either side of the boat.
Throw your top hat into the wind and set sail in your boat in the direction the wind takes you. This is the spirit of sea navigation.
Though we already encountered the kanji and element for boat, this kanji is more commonly used for medium to large sized ships, a ship large enough to fit down a 'gully'.
A person with a saw making something. Try to think of a creative use of the saw to help solidify the meaning of 'make'.

This is a play on words, the last time you 'saw' the 'sun' was yesterday. Alternatively think of the metaphorical sense of the sun being cut or 'sawed' out of the sky 'yesterday', only to reappear the day after.
Imagine a team of helpful robots that you keep on your 'shelf'. To make sure that the team are collected together, you tie a piece of 'thread' around them all.
The so-called 'power of writing' here is extended to the entire shelf. Think of how shelves have helped people throughout the ages.
This kanji is a bit abstract, so there are many interpretations on how it can represent 'craft'. Perhaps it is a crafting table or pottery wheel, a tool to plough the ground or a carpenter's square.
A 'house' with the element for 'eight' below it. The 'eight' here continues the theme of something being parted. Here we see a hole being parted in the roof of a 'house'.
Here, we see the crafting table taking up the bottom position. Above it we see a 'hole', presumably produced by the craftsperson to the let the light in and illuminate their crafting table.
We do research to fill in the academic 'holes' of things that are 'not quite' understood.
A 'house' that houses 'a hundred' people is of course an inn. Think of a busy inn with a hundred rooms housing a hundred people.

If you used the picture of a crafting table in your mind for the kanji for 'craft', this kanji can be seen as a pictogram of that same crafting table with a lump of soil or clay on it, with the meaning of the kanji focusing on the soil on top. Take care with the stroke order with this kanji. This kanji has three strokes, with the first horizontal stroke being shorter than the final horizontal stroke.

This kanji represents a company as an organisation. Unfortunately this company is very hierarchical, with the higher ups being placed on a figurative 'altar', and the employees being treated no better than the 'earth' at their feet.
A street here is represented by a simple street sign.
Here we see the very bare necessetities for a town. These being a rice field with a street running alongside it.

If you've learned any amount of Japanese, you'll probably have encountered the word for 'what'. But it's 'possible', that not every 'person' has. When asked whether it would be possible for a person to learn over 2000 kanji, their first thought would likely be 'WHAT'?!
This form is a heavily styalised pictogram of a bow that you migh use for archery. Take good care with the stroke order of this kanji's three strokes.
What else would you use to pull on a 'bow' than a 'walking stick'. Alternatively, see this as visualisation of a bow being pulled taught.

Ordinal does not seem like a very common idea to introduce so early on, but this kanji represents the nth item in an ordering. For example, 第１ represents the first, 第２ represents the second and so on. Imagine a sequence of 'bows' and their 'walking sticks' arranged in a line. Attached to each is a 'bamboo' tag and a piece of ribbon (the final stroke) which tells us which order to put the bows in: first, second, third, and so on.
Where would we be with a bow but no arrow. Of course the form has become heavily styalised, with the arrow head being turned into 'lie down'.
Here we have a new method for delivering information. You write all that you know onto an 'arrow' and fire it into someone's 'mouth'.
Under the pretense of Gratitude, this organisation 'hooks' their faithful into feeling obliged to visit the 'altar'. Don't you want to show you're gratitude by visiting the altar?
This kanji represents an administrative region, known in Japan as a prefecture. The government keeps an 'eye' on each prefecture, and consequently a metaphorical 'small hook' on each of its citizens.

This kanji can be used for both the temporal sense of doing something straightaway, but also physical sense of directly. After a difficult breakup, imagine someone collecting photos of their ex and putting 'crosses' in their 'eyes' and hanging the photos on the end of a 'hook'.
When you think of a plant, one often thinks of a 'tree straightaway' as the first example.
A doctor carries a single 'arrow' in their 'first aid box'. Back before modern injections were commonplace, medicines were instead administered via tipped arrows from a first aid box.

In this kanji, we see the legal requirement for every district to have one accessible 'first aid box'. However, instead of useful medicine inside, this box just contains a 'sheaf' of the district's local produce.
The kanji for Spirit contains the element of 'spirit' which gives the element its name. This kanji adds the element of 'sheaf', so imagine a sheaf of laurels presumably held by the spirit.
One can imagine the water vapour rising up from water as being equivalent to the invisible 'spirit' of 'water'.
Here, someone is Defeated and forced to pay up a wad of tightly 'bound up shells' to the winner.
The kanji for colour is represented here by pieces of a 'mosaic bound up' tightly.
A 'small broom' that you have to Hit with a 'small' tap to get the debris off.
Imagine a bundle of 'bound up brooms' all tightly held together and stored upright. Now imagine the 'heart' stopping sound of all those brooms suddenly falling over all at once.
Here, imagine a 'person' standing on a street corner waving about a 'spoon' and demanding for Change.

This unusual kanji shows 'two spoons' back to back which has come to mean 'north'. The spoon on the left has a different and unique form. Since it's cold in the north, imagine someone rubbing two spoons together trying to generate a spark in order to start a fire.
A simple pictogram of a plate or dish.
Here, a 'drop' of blood rests on top of a 'plate', perhaps due to an unfortunate kitchen mishap... or some other reason.
The kanji for Warm is here represented by the act of placing a 'wet dish' out in the 'sun'. The warmth from the sun will surely dry the plate.

These three strokes represent a 'measurement'. You may want to see it as a pictogram of some height measuring aparatus consisting of a moveable rod to measure someone's height. Don't forget the drop that has come detached from the measurer.
To get into this village, you have to be a certain height. Not only do they make you 'measure' your height, you then have to stand next to a 'tree'.
If you want to Protect something in your 'house', seal all the doors shut with 'glue'.
When someone gets Chastised, imagine what has been 'said' sticking to them like 'glue'
We've previously seen the kanji and element for 'oneself', and now that element is extended to include the entire body.
'Somebody' who was chastised in the earlier frame (recall the chastising words sticking to them like glue) is now demanding that they Apologise for their harmful words.
Japan is home to many ancient Buddhist temples, many of which are so old that to keep them standing, people have started 'glueing' the buildings to the 'earth'.
In ancient times, the 'temples' were in charge of keeping Time for the local community by tracking the movement of the 'sun'.

This kanji refers to things being of a certain level or Class and is also associated with equality. 'Temples' get classed based on the age of the 'bamboo' on their grounds, with older 'temples' containing older 'bamboo' obviously ranking in a higher class.
A Poem here is depicted as 'words' recounted at a 'temple'.

A 'person' here is Using something the measure the 'length' of a hole, here represented by a 'mouth'. Note the stroke order of the right side part of this kanji and how the mouth is formed inside the 'measurement' element.

Once again, we have the combination of 'mouth' and 'length', except that the first stroke of length has been omitted. Someone reciting Japan's long History at 'length', and is taking so long that no 'one' person is there anymore.
The kanji used for writing contains a 'brush' above a 'sun'. Consider the idea of someone saving their writing for when the 'sun' is out to maximise visibility.
This kanji refers to the traditional writing 'brushes' used to write Japanese characters which are often made from a stick of 'bamboo'
What is mightier, the brush or the sword? This pictogram of a sword has become heavily styalised. Be sure to keep the strokes distinct from the similar 'power' kanji and element.

Here we have a depiction of the famous 'Sword in the Stone' A Shining 'sword' is stuck into a hole in the ground here represented by the 'mouth'. Of course, the 'sword' is reflecting the rays of the 'sun', shining brightly.
A 'sword' being used to slice something and Cut it 'into pieces' is here used to represent the action of Cutting.

Similar to the last frame, here the sword is cutting something 'apart' into Parts. This kanji is more about the act of dividing something into smaller, more manageable pieces as opposed to the act of cutting itself.
Hometown here is represented by a 'rice field' and 'soil' to represent humble beginnings. However, note how the rice field and soil elements combine to create an entirely new form.
An old desktop 'computer' has here been thrown onto a 'fire' and become charred and Black. Even the screen has gone Black.

As 'computers' continue to get lighter, they increasingly need to be fasted to the desk with a Heavy 'stake' Whether forcing a heavy 'stake' through the top of a 'computer' would affect the performance, I'll leave that judgement up to the user.
A pretty straightfoward combination, someone using all their 'power' to Move a 'heavy' object. Really imagine someone with flexing arms pushing against a heavy object, trying to get it to move.
This kanji refers to a corner or angle of a shape and combines 'bound up', 'moon' and 'rice field' into a unique form.
This kanji shows a 'cow' having its 'horn' cut off by a 'sword'. Over time, the notion of removing something was abstracted to mean 'removing a problem', or Solving something.
Here we see a morbid display of bones arranged in a 'row'. The 'sword' provides the context and how the bones were seperated from their bodies.
The top part of 'bone' here extends to the right to cover a 'spoon'. If you replace all the 'bones' in your body with 'spoons', you would quickly succumb to Death.
If we consider the right-hand side of this kanji as a candlestick, the kanji's meaning of Extinguish becomes immediately apart when you introduce the 'water' element on the left.
An eye with human legs. Imagine that the eyes can't See round a corner, so grow human legs to run out and See something for themselves.
A cow with human legs. In a Previous era, humans actually evolved from 'cows'. It started with their 'human legs' before the rest of the human features appeared.
Something small with human legs. Imagine the small rays of light flittering away from a light source like 'small human legs'.
Two veritcal lines with human legs means Origin. An origin story often starts with 'two' pairs of 'human legs'.
A mouth with human legs has come to mean Older Brother. Perhaps this is a loud mouthed older brother who has the tendency to run his mouth.

A 'teenager' at an altar is obviously Celebrating some sort of coming of age ceremony or graduation. Just remember to relate your mnemonic to 'celebration' and not something like a general ceremony or ritual.
After covering the human legs, we now have a kanji relating to standing up with the emphasis again of the two straight legs standing on the ground.
A parent is someone who keeps watch and 'sees' us as we climb and eventually 'stand up' at the top of a 'tree'. Parents, of course, have a variety of responsibilities, but this kanji focuses on one.
The young Juvenile that was previously standing on top of a tree, is now 'standing' on top of a 'computer'.
A person 'standing' on top of the 'sun' would definitely make a very loud Sound.

Is this 'sound' and 'ten' or 'stand up' and 'early'? Perhaps you get up and 'stand up early' to read the first chapter, and by the time you've reached the final chapter you hear your clock 'sounding ten' o'clock at night.
When you have a good Idea, you can literally hear the 'sound' of your 'heart' beating with excitement.
When it's Dark, you either need one of two things, your own mini 'sun' or just rely on the 'sounds' around you.
The visual of Winter here is 'walking legs' slipping on two strokes representing the 'ice'.
Imagine a 'winter' jumper with a loose 'thread'. You keep pulling and pulling on the 'thread' and by the time you get to the End of it, 'winter' itself has ended.
In the middle of the Night, you hear a 'person' shouting and banging on a 'pot lid'. You run outside with your 'walking legs' to see a single 'drop' of blood on the floor.

The top of this kanji has a parallel to the kanji Hundred but with an extra stroke. In the summer, instead of slipping on ice, here the 'walking legs' are carrying 'oneself' into the shade provided by the 'ceiling' at the top.
Imagine a line of commuters all walking with their 'walking legs' to work. Each one has a 'mouth', from which come their own thoughts, hopes and beliefs.
A good host treats 'each' Guest in their 'house' uniquely, but always with great respect.
Here we have a craftsperson who has cut the 'animal legs' off a 'shellfish' in order to turn the shells into Tools. You can see the horizontal line showing the cut off 'animal legs'.

This kanji was originally meant to represent two hands acting Together to hold up an object. This kanji has a lot of twos: two vertical strokes, two horizontal strokes and two animal legs all working Together.
This kanji evokes some religious imagery of someone using a 'cross' as a 'tool' to reveal the Truth.
A person cutting up 'flesh' with their 'sword' grows a pair of 'devil horns' for some reason. Imagine them standing Before a mirror and watching the devil horns grow out.

We have seen the unique combinationf of 'bow', 'walking stick' and 'drop' in the kanji for Ordinal. Imagine an especially wicked Younger Brother with 'devil horns' playing pranks with their 'bow on a walking stick'.
Continuing with the theme of body parts, we have the kanji for the 'neck'. Imagine a grotesque image of a monster with a big 'nose', 'devil horns' and a bag of heads all cut off at the Neck.
The top part of this kanji resembles a disco ball, a 'sparkling white' object often found alongside Music. Below, we have the dancefloor made of 'wood'.

This kanji is all about good gardening techniques to keep your gardens Green. First we need to correctly section off our flower borders with garden twine or 'string' here. Then we need to sweep away any dead leaves with a 'broom'. Finally we need to include some 'sprinklers' to keep the lawn Green.
A pictogram of a hand. Although it seems to have morphed an extra finger, the original form can still be made out from the character.
You Strike down a 'nail', but end up Striking your 'finger' instead.
Imagine a monk at a 'temple' Holding something like rosary beads. Now imagine those beads intertwined round their 'fingers'.
This kanji represents the fingers themselves. A person who eats all 'day' has grown tired of using 'spoons' and has just resorted to using their 'fingers' instead.
A Strong archer has a good 'bow', good 'posture' shown here by their bent 'elbow' and good aim with the ability to target a single 'insect'.
We see 'two bows' here covered in 'ice' to mean Weak. Of course, a frozen 'bow' wouldn't flex very well and would make for a Weak bow.
An 'elbow' over a 'mouth'. Alternatively imagine someone resting their 'elbows' over a pedestal (here represented) by a mouth, perhaps in boredom or frustration.
An 'elbow' is a useful tool to use in Public. Imagine a busy crowd and 'elbowing' people out the way to 'split apart' the group.
Imagine going to a fancy 'house' to rub 'shoulder with the elites, but instead you end up in a cramped Room instead rubbing shoulders with 'dirt'.

You tried to Leave the room from the previous room, but the 'dirt' follows you out, creeping over the top of your 'shoulder'. Note that the soil element now appears on top and doubles up with the 'shoulder' element.
This kanji refers to Bringing Up or raising a child. When Bringing Up an 'infant', make sure it's needs are met, including that they get to sleep before the 'moon' is out.
This kanji refers to the overall control over or overall connection between a group. To make sure you have Overall control over a group of 'infants', tie their 'human legs' up together with 'thread'.

This character seems to resemble an abacus used to Calculate something. Notice the abacus in the centre, here represented by the 'eye' element, the 'bamboo' beads and the 'two hands' used to separate the beads. Note as well that the last stroke of 'eye' doubles up with 'two hands'.
A 'stone' being held steady with 'two hands' whilst we sharpen it.

We come to the kanji for Nose from which the 'oneself' element gets its alternative interpretation. Consider this as a pictogram of a nose, with the bridge represented by 'oneself', two flared nostrils represnted by 'rice field' and 'two hands' pressed into each nostril. Once again, we see a doubling up of the first stroke of 'two hands'.
The kanji from which the element gets its name. Even if we don't possess any material goods, we at least possess our own body, here represented by our 'flesh'.

Leftness is often associated with the sinister and evil. Here we see a sinister lefthander who 'possesses' the ability to perform witch 'craft'. They also possess the ability to reverse the stroke order of 'possess' and make the final stroke slightly longer as part of their sinister deeds, so don't forget this distinction with this kanji.
In contrast, rightness is often associate with the good and righteous. Not only is the usual stroke order restored, but shows that we 'possess a mouth' to voice all our righteous opinions.
To Rank finalists in a competition, a special type of medal has been invented. The 'thread' on the medal is elastic and 'extends' downwards in proportion with the wearer's Rank.
To Suck something, we naturally have to 'extend' our 'mouths' around the object.
This unusual kanji is a pictogram of leg and Foot though it's somewhat difficult to make out now.
To start your journey on a Path, it's no good to just dip one 'foot' in, you need to put 'each foot' onto the path and walk forward with confidence.
This kanji is a pictogram of an Ear. You might notice the relation with 'eye' and 'nose', though be careful with the revised stroke order here.
This kanji resembles a mouth with something sticking out of it and carries the meaning of Tongue. The thing sticking out is a 'stake', perhaps referencing a tongue piercing.
This kanji is quite self explanatory. When we Talk 'words', we move our 'tongues'.
Here we see a lively discussion with lots of 'tongues' wagging back and forth. It's so lively you can even see the drops of 'watery' saliva coming off the tongue.
This collection of strokes has come to mean 'bean'.
Imagine a very Short elf trying to collect 'beans', but they are too short to reach them and so use an 'arrow' to shoot them off.
A 'teepee' is quite useful for a quick Departure. Just collapse with your 'two hands' to take it with you. Note how the final vertical strokes of the 'two hands' instead resemble 'human legs'.
Here we see someone Climbing up the sides of their 'teepee' to get to some stored 'beans', presumably placed their to dry out in the wind.
The kanji from which the 'shape' element gets its name. Here we see 'two hands' ironing out the creases in something to restore its Shape.

You might want to think of some famous 'white cliffs' for this kanji. Then extend your pnemonic to include a 'small' Meadow, perhaps at the base of the cliffs so that you don't accidentally misplace the 'small' element.

This is a nice pictogram of a Charcoal fire being set up by the 'cliffs' at the base of a 'mountain'. Make sure you consider the fire to be strictly at the base of a cliff, and not in any sort of cave.
Two lovers driven to the edge of a 'cliff holding hands'. But what drove them to this perilous situation? Someone must have disapproved and been 'anti-' this relationship.
This kanji represents a steep Slope that runs against (or anti-) the naturally 'ground'.
A Board here is a flat piece of wood. Whoever is making all these Boards must be 'anti tree' judging by the number of trees that are needed to be cut down in order for the person to make them.
A Friend here is quite elegantly represented as two people who 'possess' the ability to 'hold hands'.
Imagine someone here 'holding the hands' of someone who needs to Take some good advice or encouragement. You can only hope that what you say actually goes into their 'ear'.

We start our stories centred on family life with a kanji representing a refined Gentleman. Note the humble relationship with the 'soil' element, except in this case, the top stroke extends over the bottom.
A 'person' standing beside a 'gentleman' here has come to carry the meaning of Service.
The calming Voice of a refined 'gentleman' here is likened to a 'mosaic'. Note the unique form of the final stroke of mosaic in this kanji.

Next in our family, we have the Woman of the house. It was originally meant to represent an unfortunate pictogram of a woman kneeling, and you can still make out the kneeled figure in the first stroke. Despite being made up of only three strokes, balancing these three strokes into an aesthetically pleasing form can be quite challenging.
Life Begins with a single 'woman' who puts their babies on metaphorical 'pedestals' so that they grow up to be strong and healthy.
Here we have a 'woman' Relaxing after a hard day of work. And where is best to Relax other than in your own 'house'.
Our humble family continues with a child. Notice its over-sized head and spreading arms of joy.
This kanji is quite straightforward. It represents a 'woman's' Fondness towards their 'child'.

With the great number of kanji Characters required to read Japanese, it is no wonder that a 'child' sitting in a 'house' came to mean the Characters themselves. Imagine a child sitting in their house writing out character after character.
This character represents a person with outstretched arms and has come to mean Big.

The only thing differentiating this kanji from the one in the previous frame is the 'drop' in the top-right corner. You might be familiar with the image of a pirate with a parrot on its shoulder, well here we have a 'giant' which is big enough to get an entire Dog on its shoulder, here represented by a single 'drop'.
This is the 'house' you take a broken things to to Determine whether it can be 'mended' or not.
The kanji from which the 'head' element gets its name. Here it is accompanied by 'beans', representing the mushy brains inside.
This complicated kanji shows a 'cliff' Face with the 'shape' of 'heads' carved into it and a person 'standing up' on top of the 'cliff' pulling funny Faces.

The Topic of a piece of writing is often laid out in its 'heading'. The rest of the document is likely full of typos and will require 'all day mending it'. See how the final stroke of 'mending' is extra long here.
The kanji that gives 'grass' its name. We have already met the combination of 'sun' and 'ten' in the kanji for Early (早). Here we see 'grass' growing early in the year to mark the dawn of spring.

We met the change-demanding spoon waver in the kanji for Change (化). This time, the activis takes the form of an environmentalist with 'grasses' in their hair and calling for the advent of Flower power.

At the customs office, the customs officer pulls some Luggage aside. It turns out that there's some suspicious 'grass' inside the case and the officer what's to know 'what' is inside. Recall that the combination of 'person' and 'possible' exists in the kanji for What (何).
Some 'grasses' have water resistant leaves that allow 'each' drop of 'water' that comes into contact with them to Fall downwards towards the roots.
The once aromatic herbacious 'grass' has become Bitter as it grows 'old'.

Once again, we must recall from a previous frame the combination of 'white', 'sparkles' and 'tree' makes for the kanji for Music (楽). We now just need to complete our story with the 'grass' element. This kanji focusses on two forms of Medicine, herbaceous 'grasses' and the holistic 'music' that acts as a form of medicine for the mind.

You may notice a 'grass'-like element hidden in this kanji, along with a 'hook'. This unique arrangement of strokes represents a freshly sprouted leaf, which came to be used as a sign of a new Generation. Another interpretation is that this kanji contains three lots of ten (十) to indicate a period of thirty years.
The kanji for Leaf itself contains the Generation kanji we just learned alongside the elements for 'grass' and 'tree' as if to really drive home their natural origins.
This kanji is used when recounting a story from long, Long Ago. It is believed that Long Ago, 'grass' took over the barren earth in just 'one day'.
The kanji for Wheat not only shows the blades of Wheat 'growing up', but also growing 'walking legs' so they can walk straight to the baker after being harvested.
This kanji references something or someone 'growing up' on the moon. The lack of oxygen there means they have turned Blue.
The kanji here refers to Clear weather. When the sky is 'blue' and the 'sun' is out, the weather is said to be Clear.

'Grow up' with a single 'drop' represents Life itself. The drop represnts that extra something that brings something to life. This kanji is infamous for the number of different readings it has but it's perhaps not as bad as it may first look.
This kanji describes a Star as being a 'sun' that has the ability to give 'life' to its planets.
During the Frigid weather, someone has insulated their 'house' by blocking all the holes with 'leeks'. Just look at how cold the 'leeks' are getting with all the 'ice' on them.
The 'leek'-filed 'house' from the previous frame is having any holes too small to fit leeks, Stuffed up with 'soil'.
This kanji refers to the actual Reality as opposed to a hypothetic scenario. The Reality of keeping a 'bonsai' is that you will have to spend a lot of time in your 'house' tending to it.
This kanji refers to season of Spring. Incidentally, spring is also the best time for 'bonsais', just imagine them sitting in the 'sun' with their Spring blossoms on show.
Autumn is the season when when leftover 'wheat' is set on 'fire' to help fertilise the land in preparation for planting the next year's crops.
This kanji is also used for Japanese things. You know when Harmony is achieved when everyone's 'mouths' are filled with enough 'wheat'.
A 'few' grains of 'wheat' was abstracted into the meaning of a 'few' moments of time, which was further refined into Second, the short unit of time.
In this society, though the menfolk would harvest the 'wheat', it was actually down to a Committee of 'women' to decide what to do with it.
This Department is responsible for making sure everyon is fed. They carefully 'measure' out the correct amount of 'wheat' to give per household.
This depiction of a small sprout coming from the ground has been abstracted to mean Reason, indicating that the Reason for something happening can ultimately be quite small.
This kanji shows the creation of vegetable Oil, just 'water' the 'sprouts' so they grow up and sprout oil.
A Flute here is a traditional one made of 'bamboo'. Only the tender stems of newly 'sprouted bamboo' are suitable for turning into flutes however.
The keyword chosen for this kanji references the humble language this kanji is often used in. It may be easier to see this kanji as something coming out of a mouth to indicate a person speaking.
The strength of a good Deity lies in their ability to 'push through' the confines of the prayer 'altar' and merge into the life and culture of their adherents.
The kanji for rice contains the kanji for 'tree' with two additional 'drops' to represent the individual grains of rice.
You may be familiar with this kanji already. Two trees together make for a grove.
Three trees together make for a whole forest. Both this kanji and the previous are a good showcase of the intuitive nature of kanji.
This kanji appears to depict a tree with a branch that has Not Yet fully grown. This has taken on the meaning of something that has not yet happened.
Flavour is the thing that we experience when put food in our 'mouths' but it has 'not yet' reached our stomaches.
A Younger Sister here is a depiction of someone who is 'not yet' a 'woman'.

The kanji used for the word 'to come' is a combination of both 'not yet' and 'rice'. Imagine people waiting impatiently for someone to Come, with the reason for their lateness being that they have 'not yet' finished their bowl of 'rice'.
This character is used to count the number of Brush Strokes in a kanji. Lower the 'sprouting' hairs of a brush into a 'bucket' of ink just 'once' and see how many Brush Strokes you can manage.
This form does loosely resemble a tooth. To put a 'stop' to Tooth decay, people moved away from eating 'rice' from 'buckets', opting for more portion controlled bowls instead.

Addressing others correctly is very important in Japan. Addressing someone with this kanji can sometimes be considered rude and as if you are talking down to them. Therefore, a person who frequently calls you 君, might appear to be a Buddy, but really ought to clean out their 'mouths' with a 'mop'.

This kanji is probably one of the few that is best learnt via rote memorisation. Luckily this is a very common kanji. Its meaning is something non physical. Imagine the 'thing' that no 'one' talks about, so everyone just keeps their 'mouths' closed and keeps mopping the floor.
This character appears to show a vertical knife cutting something in Half. The two drops show peices of the object coming away as it is cut.
The Winner of the space race gets the power to divide the 'moon' up, not just into halves but 'quarters' too.

A common but disputed etymology for this kanji is that it shows a 'sun' rising' behind a 'tree'. Regardless of whether this is the true form of the original character, this story is enough to help us memorise this kanji's meaning of East.
The merchants who traveled along the silk road were well Practiced at trading with those from the 'east' for their silk 'threads'.
This kanji shows a pictogram of flowers drooping from a plant and came to be used for the general act of Drooping.
This is another unique doubling up of 'droop' and 'tree' elements. Imagine Riding on top of some 'wooden' vehicle with your legs 'drooping' down over the sides.

This kanji appears to show an unusual doubling up of the characters for 'dog' and 'person' with the presence of an extra drop. The person here appears to have Lost their dog and is still holding on to the leash that the dog was once attached to (here represnted by the drop-like stroke).

The kanji here for 'red' contains a few more unique strokes at the bottom. Ignoring the stroke order, the form bares a resemblence to the 'sword' element, with little drops of Red 'blood' either side.

The kanji for yellow contains some more natural elements, 'animal legs', some 'grass' and 'one sprout'. This sounds like a meal that few would want to eat, so imagine the grass and sprout wilting and turning Yellow.
Though we won't see the form of 'yellow' often enough to regard it as an element, it does recur in this kanji. A 'tree' that has fallen over and turned Horizontal, also has 'yellow' leaves.
Staring the chapter on animal-based elements is a kanji consisting of a pictogram for Feathers
We see a pair of 'feathers' over a 'white' piece of paper to display the covery the meaning of Learn.
At this Gathering, people Gather round a 'tree' and celebrate by eating a 'turkey' which, bizarrely, is placed on top of the tree.

This is an ancient way of counting the Days Of The Week. Each 'day' you pluck out a couple of 'feathers' from a 'turkey' to keep track. Notice that the 'feathers' here become contracted into a pair of 'ヨ's.
You might be used to a bell tolling at Noon, but here we have a 'flute' that is blown just 'once a day' at Noon.
The kanji for Horse has a similar form to 'turkey' with the addition of four galloping legs and a tail.

The outline of this kanji has a striking resemblance to JR, the name initials given to the Japanese Railway Group. Traditionally, to communicate that a train was on its way to the Station, they a 'horse'-riding flautist would play a melody on their 'flute'.

When playing a song on a 'flute', the flautist can make their own Interpretation. Now imagine them sitting outside summoning animals with the sweet sounds of their flute-playing, as referenced by the 'animal tracks'.

Earlier we met the kanji 第 given the unusual keyword of 'Ordinal'. Now we have 'Serial'. This involves counting things in a ranked order. 一番 is first place, 二番 is second place etc. This kanji involves a competition to see who can be the best at mimicing 'animal tracks' in a 'rice field'.
From the previous frame, we have to consider the chance of a tie in the 'animal tracks in a rice field' contest. Instead of Flipping a coin, we here Flip two 'feathers' to determine the winner.
The character for bird is also a loose pictogram of a bird. Notice the relationship with 'horse' with the final five strokes.
A 'bird' Chirping with its open 'mouth'. This kanji not only covers the sounds from birds, but other animals and even other things that might sound such as alarms and telephones.

This unusual kanji instead replaces the four final strokes in 'bird' with a 'mountain'. Imagine a 'bird' on a remote Island which has evolved a unique display of feathers to help it perch onto the island's 'mountain'.
The elements for this kanji are 'bound up', 'rice field', 'fire', which together form the image of a Fish with fins being represented by the four strokes normally associate with 'fire'.
This is the kanji from which we got the 'house' element's name from. Recall the story of the Three Little 'Pigs' who each built their 'house' out of a different material.
This is the kanji generally used for Pigs and also 'pig flesh', more commonly known as pork.
Imagine that Place you always wanted to visit. Now imagine the joy of smashing your 'piggy bank' onto the 'earth' to release the cash when you have finally saved up enough money.
A 'piggy bank' is actually quite useful for boiling 'water'. Just put it over the stove and heat to get Hot Water.
No-one wants to sleep on the Ground floor, not only is there where the 'soil' gets brought in on people's shoes, but it's also susceptible to attacks from 'scorpions'.
We just saw that the ground was full of 'scorpions', but the waters are not safe either. Imagine a 'pond' filled with 'scorpions' that have adapted to life in the 'water'.
Imagine the 'person' you attributed to the person element swinging on a vine over a pit of 'scoprions' to get to the Other side.
This kanji reminds me of the story of St Patrick banishing all the 'snakes' from Irelend. Presumably he brought all the 'snakes together' at the Harbour and threw them all into the 'water'.
Since 'snakes' can't write they have to Record their own 'words' using a tape Recorder.
This form represents a Sheep with two little sheep horns.
This kanji seems to reference the French fairy tale about a Beauty and a beast, who here is depicted as a 'big' 'horned ram'.
We saw this combination of 'mop' and 'mouth' previously in the kanji for Buddy. Here we imagine our 'buddy' sheepdog rounding up a Group of 'sheep'.

It's rare that we will encounter a Japanese keyword, but there is no good English translation for this word. This word is used as suffix when addressing someone of great respect, usually reserved for a deity or the emperor. Imagine the people, here represented by 'sheep', showing respect to a great magical 'tree' deity 'tree'-Sama by showering its roots with holy water from 'sprinklers'.
This kanji depicts a plucky 'sheep' who jumped in the 'water' and swam from Overseas all the way to Japan.

Occasionally we will see that the tail of the sheep returns in the form of an extra stroke. Here we see a shepherd keeping an 'eye' on his 'sheep' waiting for their wool to grow long enough so that they can be shorn and the wool turned into something to Wear.

Another kanji closely related with the evening. Japanese tradition states that instead of a there being a man in the moon, there is a 'rabbit' in the moon. When the 'sun' sets, the moon-'rabbit' appears for the start of Nightfall.
Imagine a 'rabbit' working on its burrow using its 'powerful' hind legs to hollow out its new home.

This kanji depicts a 'holding hand', this time holding onto some fur and pulling it from some animal pelt. The kanji came to carry the meaning of the Pelt left behind. As usual, take care with the order and direction of the strokes.
This kanji likens the Wave on the surface of 'water' being like a 'pelt'.

This is the first kanji in the word for kanji, representing the 'kan' part. We already encountered 'ji' (字) as Character in a previous chapter. Rice and rice argriculture was brought to Japan from China, and with it came the Chinese 'water scarecrows' standing in the wet paddies.
The 'scarecrows' are good keeping away smaller birds, but to keep away the larger 'turkeys', it is much more Difficult.

The top of this kanji resembles the element for 'house' but instead uses four strokes on top instead of the usual one. Together we will attribute 'birdhouse' as the meaning of this form. Then we have the 'holding hands' seemingly holding the 'birdhouse'. Imagine someone has Received a 'birdhouse' as some sort of unusual gift.

We end the chapter learning the kanji for Love itself. We see some metaphorical Love birds in a metaphorical 'birdhouse', though their 'hearts' may occasionally wander on 'walking legs', they always return to their true Love.

We start with our humble Someone. This Someone is heavily reliant on the very 'earth' we walk and their schedule is largely governed by the 'sun'. Not the extra stroke that connects the two elements together.
The unremarkably 'someone' can here be seen toiling under the 'sun'. Just imagine how Hot they must be feeling.
The cruel 'taskmaster' is here asking this poor 'woman' to count the Number of grains of 'rice' they have.

If you imagined a particularly strict teacher as your taskmaster, this kanji will be quite easy to remember. The 'taskmaster' is Teaching 'someone's child' a very importnat lesson. Or at least it is very important to the taskmaster.

A 'sprinkler', a 'ceiling' and a 'single drop' takes on the meaning of Request. You pull the fire alarm and set off the 'sprinklers' on the 'ceiling', but you Request goes unanswered, and all you get is a single 'drop'.
When you're in a truly dire situation, sometime the only thing that will Rescue you will be a 'request' for help from the 'taskmaster'.
Imagine your 'person' being helped out by the very helpful 'porter'. It is of course the 'porter's' Duty to be helpful.
This kanji appears similar to 'request', but all those drops and sparkles are replaced with a single 'drop'. This is the Genius, a very hard-working scholarly individual.
Another someone unique arrangements of strokes is used for the meaning of Surname.
At the end of the Paper, you need to sign your 'surname'. Then put a bit of 'thread' round the whole thing and post it.

On the right we have a 'tree' with a very large 'crown'. The 'human legs' here are more long leggy branches that hold the crown of the tree up. To sustain such a large tree, the roots must go Deep into the ground to find 'water'.
The 'gentleman' here is Selling a 'crown'. Instead of it costing him an arm and a leg to acquire, it instead costed him two 'human legs'.
The 'seller' from the previous frame should Read the 'words' enscribed on the crown he was trying to sell. 'Not to be sold seprately'.
We have risen through the ranks and arrived at the kanji for King.
The 'king' with a 'drop' beneath his robe. The drop of course represents the king's precious Jewel.
If there's one way to describe a 'computer' it would be that they are the 'king' of Logic.
Closely related to the 'king', is the Master denoted by the extra 'drop' on his head as a sign of allegiance to the king.
The place where your 'person' spends the 'main' part of their day is at their Dwelling where they can be the 'master' of the house.
Imagine a small hut with a single 'wooden' Pillar in the centre. This piece of 'wood' is the 'main' thing holding the whole thing up.
The 'king' made a 'request' to get his jewel polished, but the polisher was a bit too enthusiastic and managed to polish it into a Sphere.
Whatever you do, don't Pour 'water' onto the 'main' electrical supply as this kanji would suggest. Obviously!
This Institution is 'housed' at the 'pinnacle' and is really the perfect place to be. Like all well-reputed establishments. It has a long 'origin' story.

The double spoons is actually 'compare' which we have met previously. The 'pinnacle' is so high up, you're several Storeys above the 'white' clouds and get to 'compare' yourself (favourably of course) to everyone down below.
Seeing the Sunshine from atop the 'pinnacle' is a beautiful sight, but unfortunately getting the privilege requires you to empty all your 'piggy banks'.

We have finalled ascended all the way up through the crown, the king, and the pinnacle to the final highest place, Heaven. The interpretation is that this kanji represents a person with a big flat head.
A 'jewel' (玉) that has been 'pent in' here represents a Country. Here the 'jewel' represents the entire Country, and the surrounding enclosure represents the coutry's borders.

This kanji has an iterative nature, a square within a square. Imagine zooming into the inner square to find another square inside. No matter what Number of Times you zoom in, you still see the same kanji.
Here we have a Drawing of the 'big dipper' collection of stars. However, due to the size of the page, the Drawing has had to be 'pent in' and has been crushed a bit, altering its appearace.
When caving, you want to pick a 'cave' that's Wide enough to fit your 'elbows' in at the side of your body, otherwise you might get stuck.
We see a mysterious little Store in the middle of a 'cave'. Imagine the loud 'mouthed' storekeeper trying to sell their supply of suspicious 'magic wands'.

Here we have a 'cave', some people 'holding hands' and what appears to be a lantern hanging from the season. Imagine some miners in a cold 'cave' huddling around a lantern and 'holding hands' with each other to keep warm. 'How many Degrees is it?' They mutter to each other.
This kanji is a pictogram of a cart with two large wheels at the top and bottom and central vertical axil running through everything.
No-one quite knows where, but in a 'cave' somewhere there's a Warehouse where they make all the 'cars' in the world.
Due to the increasing number of 'ditches' about, people are now opting for more Lightweight 'cars'. The heavier ones tend to get stuck in the ditches.
When it feels like your stuck a 'ditch', don't depair. It's not forever and you just need to Pass Through it. If you can, search for a 'thread' of hope to pull you out of the 'ditch'.
The kanji for Enter differs from Person by having the right stroke longer than the left. Note the appearance of a person stepping into somewhere as if Entering.
The kanji for Exit consists of 'two mountains' doubled up. The only way to Exit the valley is on this narrow path between 'two mountains'.
This kanji is a pictogram of a Gate and carries the same meaning. The two doors of the Gate have been places higher up, creating space for another element to occupy.
At the 'pearly gates', a 'mouth' asks you many Questions about your life to judge whether you may pass to heaven or not.
At the 'pearly gates', they go through your whole life history, going through each 'day' and judging the whole Interval.
After asking you questions, they then Hear your plee at the 'pearly gates' as to why you should be let in. To do this, imagine a giant 'ear' appearing.
Once they've judged you for your sins, you're free to 'hold you hand' and Open the 'pearly gates' themselves, guiding you into the afterlife.

The security is very tight at the 'pearly gates'. They don't let anyone in who isn't properly vetted, and even have a 'genius' stationed at the front of the gates who is wise to all sorts of tricks, to make sure the gates remain Closed
This kanji focuses on the 'gatekeeper' at the 'pearly gates' and their overall Connection, not just to life and death, but heaven and hell too.
You're on a road, and you want to 'enter' the next lane but it's just too Crowded to get in.
Though the element means 'road', this is the general kanji for a Road. Think of a bottle 'neck', the result of poorly designed 'road' planning, where too many roads coalesce into one.
The 'gatekeeper' here is standing at the beginning of a toll 'road'. They don't let you through until you Send them the correct money.
How do you Return after you've been on the 'road' somewhere? This kanji would suggest that you take the 'anti road'.

As a sign of Progress, not only are there pedestrian crossings for humans on the 'road', but now for 'turkeys' too. Just imagine a green turkey appearing to indicate that a turkey can safely cross the road.
A 'car with a crown on' appears to be some sort of armoured vehicle. Now consider this armed vehicle Carrying a supply of aid or perhaps weapons along a designated 'road'.

At an election, we look out on the metaphorical 'road' that is our future and our faced with two candidates to Choose between. But unfortunately whoever we end up Choosing, it appears both politicians are 'snakes' and working 'together' anyway.
The 'taskmaster' is a ruthless micromanager and demands everything be Organised by placing everything into 'bundles' and checking that it is all 'correct'.
This kanji represents a post officer carrying a big 'bundle'. Presumably this is a first-class 'bundle' as it has to be delivered Fast.

Before Building can even commence, modern laws require scrupulous health and safety checks. The legal team brings forth a 'stretcher' full of health and safety documents asking you to sign them all with a (company provided) 'brush'.

A 'porter' in an enclosure... in another enclosure. Unfortunately the 'porter carrying the very important thing' has been attacked. Here he is lying on a 'stretcher' in a 'cave'. Medics quickly take him to the medical Yard to try to save him.
